content: Long-term treatment of schizophrenia with typical antipsychotic medications has significant limitations, as approximately 25-33% of patients exhibit treatment-resistant forms of the illness. Clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic, is reported to have superior efficacy in such cases and is associated with fewer motor-related adverse effects compared to typical antipsychotics. However, clozapine carries a substantial risk of serious hematological complications, such as agranulocytosis, necessitating mandatory weekly blood monitoring, particularly during the initial months of treatment. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of clozapine with those of typical antipsychotic drugs in individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia. For this purpose, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were analyzed, and data were extracted independently. Dichotomous outcomes were assessed using relative risks (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI), while continuous outcomes were evaluated using weighted mean differences (WMD). Numbers needed to treat (NNT) or harm (NNH) were calculated where applicable. A total of 52 trials involving 4,746 participants were included in this review. Most of these studies (44 trials) were short-term, lasting less than 13 weeks, and were found to have a significant risk of bias. No significant differences were observed between clozapine and typical antipsychotics in terms of broad outcomes such as mortality, ability to work, or readiness for discharge at the end of the study period. However, clinical improvements were more frequently observed in patients treated with clozapine (14 RCTs, n=1,119, RR 0.72, CI 0.7 to 0.8, NNT 6, CI 5 to 8). Additionally, clozapine-treated participants experienced fewer relapses compared to those on typical antipsychotics (n=1,303, RR 0.62, CI 0.5 to 0.8, NNT 21, CI 15 to 49). Symptom reduction, as measured by the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS), was greater in the clozapine group (17 RCTs, n=1,205, WMD -3.79, CI -4.9 to -2.7), although the data were heterogeneous (I²=69%). Short-term improvements in negative symptoms, as assessed by the Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS), also favored clozapine (6 RCTs, n=196, WMD -7.21, CI -8.9 to -5.6). Furthermore, clozapine was found to be more acceptable for long-term treatment compared to typical antipsychotics (6 RCTs, n=982, RR 0.60, CI 0.5 to 0.7, NNT 15, CI 12 to 20). Adverse effects were more common in the clozapine group. Blood-related complications, such as agranulocytosis, occurred in 3.2% of clozapine-treated participants compared to 0% in those receiving typical antipsychotics (13 RCTs, n=1,031, RR 7.09, CI 2.0 to 25.6). Other side effects, including drowsiness, hypersalivation, and fever, were also more frequent in the clozapine group. However, clozapine was associated with significantly fewer motor-related adverse effects (19 RCTs, n=1,495, RR 0.57, CI 0.5 to 0.7, NNT 5, CI 4 to 6). In patients resistant to typical antipsychotics, clozapine demonstrated more pronounced clinical benefits. These included higher rates of clinical improvement (4 RCTs, n=370, RR 0.71, CI 0.6 to 0.8, NNT 4, CI 3 to 6) and greater symptom reduction. Notably, 34% of treatment-resistant participants showed clinical improvement with clozapine. In conclusion, clozapine appears to be more effective than typical antipsychotics in reducing symptoms of schizophrenia, achieving clinically meaningful improvements, and delaying relapse. However, the data are limited and prone to bias. While participants generally expressed greater satisfaction with clozapine treatment, its benefits in the short term do not necessarily translate into improvements in global functioning, such as the ability to leave the hospital or maintain employment. The risks of adverse effects, particularly hematological complications, must be carefully weighed against its benefits. These risks appear to be higher in children, adolescents, and the elderly compared to young or middle-aged adults. Importantly, existing trials have largely overlooked the perspectives of patients and their families regarding clozapine treatment. More long-term, community-based randomized trials are needed to evaluate the impact of clozapine on global and social functioning, as well as its efficacy in special populations, such as individuals with learning disabilities.
